title: Stereotypes and Individual Differences
keyIdea: A stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified idea that everyone in a group is the same, for example because of their gender, race, age or religion. Stereotypes are unfair because they ignore individual differences: people inside any group differ far more from each other than the group differs from another group. One counter-example, a real person who does not fit, shows an all-or-never idea is wrong. Nice-sounding stereotypes still put a label on people.

kid: A stereotype is an idea that everyone in a group is the same. Boys don't cry. Girls aren't good at maths. Old people can't use phones. The group might be about gender, age, race or religion.

Stereotypes are unfair because people are not copies. Some boys love football, and some love ballet or chess. The label fits a few people and is wrong about the rest. That is called ignoring individual differences.

You can break a stereotype with a counter-example. That is one real person who does not fit. Amira is a girl who won the maths contest. Leo is a boy who cried when his dog died. One person is enough to show an all idea is wrong.
Watch out for nice ones too. People who wear glasses are clever sounds kind, but it is still one label for a whole group. When you hear a stereotype, stay calm and name a person it leaves out.
adult: This topic is part of the IB PYP PSPE identity strand. It also fits PSHE Relationships lessons at Key Stage 2. Pupils learn that stereotypes can be based on gender, race, religion, age or disability. They learn that stereotypes are unfair and can hurt. The skills are to define a stereotype, say why one is wrong, and challenge it with a counter-example.

The key idea is variation. In the lab's sample class, girls' maths scores run from 4 to 19 and boys' from 3 to 19. Yet the two averages differ by only 0.2. Real data looks like this too. A 2008 study in Science looked at over seven million US pupils aged about 7 to 17. It found no real gap between girls and boys in maths tests.

Common mistakes: thinking a stereotype is fine if it is true of some people, and thinking a compliment can't be a stereotype. Another is a weak counter-example. Some boys like maths does not answer girls can't do maths. A fourth is answering with insults, which makes views harder. Studies of stereotype threat show labels can pull down the scores of the people they describe.

In the lab your child flips twelve boys labelled loves football and counts how many fit. They drag the right person onto three stereotypes and slide two groups of maths scores into one line. Then they find four stereotypes in a list of eight and pick calm replies to one said out loud.

familyTip: When an advert, a film or a friend says 'boys always…' or 'girls never…', ask your child: 'Can you think of one person who doesn't fit?' Naming a real person is the quickest way to break a stereotype.

visual.caption: Stereotype or not? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

bins: 🏷️ Stereotype: one label for a whole group
👤 Not a stereotype: a person or a fact
items: Old people can't learn new things.
Leo cried at the end of the film.
Some children in my class like chess.
Amira is in the maths club.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: flip labelled cards, break stereotypes with counter-examples, mix two groups' scores and reply calmly.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a stereotype?
choices: Our class did a maths test today.
practice.hint: A stereotype puts one idea on a whole group of people.
practice.explain: Girls aren't good at maths says a whole group is the same. The others are about one person or a fact.

practice.prompt: A class has {n} boys. Someone says all boys love football. How many boys must dislike football to break that idea?
practice.hint: How many counter-examples does it take to show an all idea is wrong?
practice.explain: Just 1. One boy who doesn't love football is a counter-example, so all boys love football is false, even in a class of {n}.

practice.prompt: Someone says old people can't use phones. Which is a counter-example?
choices: Grandad Ray, 74, runs a video channel
practice.hint: Find a real old person who uses phones or tech.
practice.explain: Grandad Ray is old and uses tech every day, so he proves the idea wrong. Knitting says nothing about phones.

practice.prompt: In one class, girls' maths scores run from {a} to 19 out of 20. What is the gap between the lowest and highest girl?
practice.hint: Take the lowest score away from the highest.
practice.explain: 19 − {a} = {=19-a}. A gap of {=19-a} inside one group is much bigger than the 0.2 gap between the girls' and boys' averages.

choices: A fixed idea that everyone in a group is the same
A rule that keeps people safe
pool.hint: Think of boys don't cry. Who is it about?
pool.explain: A stereotype is a fixed idea that everyone in a group is the same. It ignores individual differences.

choices: They are always about bad things
They are only said by adults
pool.hint: Remember the twelve boys in the lab.
pool.explain: People in any group are all different. A stereotype treats them as copies, so it is wrong about many of them.

pool.prompt: People who wear glasses are clever. Is this a stereotype?
choices: Yes, it labels a whole group
pool.hint: Does it say everyone in a group is the same?
pool.explain: Yes. Even a compliment is a stereotype if it puts one label on a whole group.

pool.prompt: Ella says girls can't catch. What is the best reply?
choices: Priya catches loads in netball. Let her try.
pool.hint: Use a counter-example and stay calm.
pool.explain: Naming Priya is a calm counter-example. Insults start a fight and silence lets the stereotype stand.

pool.prompt: Someone says boys don't cry. Which fact breaks it?
choices: Leo, 10, cried when his dog died
pool.hint: You need a boy who cries.
pool.explain: Leo is a boy who cried, so he is a counter-example. Girls crying says nothing about boys.

pool.prompt: In a class of 30, {n} children love chess. Is it a stereotype to say some children in my class like chess?
choices: No, it is a true fact about some people
Yes, it is about a group
Yes, because chess is a game
pool.hint: Does it say every child is the same?
pool.explain: No. Some is not all, and {n} children really do like chess, so it does not label the whole class.

pool.prompt: Twelve boys are labelled loves football, but only {k} of them do. For how many boys is the label wrong?
pool.hint: Take the boys it fits away from all twelve.
pool.explain: 12 − {k} = {=12-k}. The label is wrong for {=12-k} boys, which is why stereotypes are unfair.

pool.prompt: Girls' and boys' maths scores in one class overlap from 4 to 19. What does that show?
choices: You can't tell a person's score from their group
pool.hint: Think of the mixed-up line in the lab.
pool.explain: The scores mix all the way through, so knowing someone is a girl or a boy tells you almost nothing about their score.
